titleEn: The Song of the Cid — Ximena glad, the Cid wary; the weddings in Valencia (tiradas 109–111, lines 2190–2277)
part: Tiradas 109–111 · Ximena glad, the Cid wary; the weddings in Valencia (lines 2190–2277)

sentences.t:
Besáronle las manos la mugier e las fijas
e todas las dueñas [de quien son servidas]:
sentences.l:
Kissed-him the hands the wife and the daughters
and all the ladies [by whom they are served]:
sentences.i: His wife and his daughters kissed his hands, and so did all the ladies who wait on them:
sentences.n: Tirada 109 (assonance í-a) — Doña Ximena and her daughters are well content (Pidal: Doña Jimena y las hijas se muestran satisfechas). The line-ends run fijas, servidas, vellida, guisa, días, ricas: stressed í, then a. Besáronle = besaron + le, 'they kissed him … the hands', the hands named after the pronoun: the kiss of thanks and homage. la mugier, 'the wife' (mugier = mujer), Ximena. dueñas, the ladies of her household. The whole second half of v. 2191, de quien son servidas, 'by whom they are served', is Pidal's restoration (in italics); the manuscript gives only the first half-line.

sentences.t:
“Grado al Criador e a vos, Çid, barba vellida!
todo lo que vos feches es de buena guisa.
Non serán menguadas en todos vuestros días!”
sentences.l:
“Thanks to-the Creator and to you, Çid, beard handsome!
all that which you do is of good manner.
Not they-shall-be diminished in all your days!”
sentences.i: “Thanks be to the Creator, and to you, Çid of the handsome beard! All that you do is well done. They shall want for nothing all your days!”
sentences.n: The women speak together. Grado, 'thanks' (as at v. 2187). barba vellida, 'handsome beard', the epithet that stands for the Çid himself, here in the vocative: 'Çid, (you of) the handsome beard' (vellida = bellida). feches = fazedes, 'you do'. Pidal's note: 'todo lo que vos hacéis está bien hecho', 'everything you do is well done'; de buena guisa, 'of a good fashion'. Non serán menguadas, 'they shall not be in want' (menguar, 'to fall short, lack'): the feminine plural most likely means the daughters, now well provided for; en todos vuestros días, 'all your days', as long as you live.

sentences.t: —“Quando vos nos casáredes bien seremos ricas.”
sentences.l: —“When you us shall-marry well we-shall-be rich.”
sentences.i: “When you marry us off, we shall be rich indeed.”
sentences.n: Pidal's dash marks a new speaker: the daughters answer. casáredes, future subjunctive of casar in the time clause, 'when you shall marry (us)': the father marries his daughters off. nos, 'us', the object, before the verb. Tirada 109 ends here.

sentences.i: “Doña Ximena, my wife, thanks be to the Creator. To you I say it, my daughters, Doña Elvira and Doña Sol: from this marriage of yours we shall grow in lands and lordship;
sentences.n: Tirada 110 (assonance ó) — the Çid's misgivings about the marriage (Pidal: El Cid recela del casamiento). The line-ends run Criador, Sol, onor, yo, Alfons, coraçón, no, ados, yo. Pidal's rubric reads a misgiving the Çid never puts into words: what he says, twice (vv. 2199 and 2204), is that the match is the king's doing and not his own. Mugier doña Ximena, 'wife Doña Ximena', a formal address. don Elvira, so printed (don, not doña), as at v. 2163; 'Doña Elvira' in the English. deste = de + este. vu[e]stro and creçr[e]mos: in each word the single e is Pidal's restoration, read as italic at the limit of the scan's resolution, so these two brackets are the least sure readings of the part. creçremos = creceremos, 'we shall grow', the future with its middle vowel dropped (as creçrá at v. 1905). onor here is lands and lordship held, kept distinct from ondra 'honour': the Çid takes up the king's own words, abrá y ondra e creçrá en onor (v. 1905).

sentences.t:
mas bien sabet verdad que non lo levanté yo:
pedidas vos ha e rogadas el mio señor Alfons,
atan firme mientre e de todo coraçón
que yo nulla cosa nol sope dezir de no.
sentences.l:
but well know truth that not it raised I:
asked you has and begged my lord Alfons,
so firm -ly and of all heart
that I no thing not-to-him could say of no.
sentences.i: but know this for the truth: it was not I who set it on foot. My lord Alfonso has asked for you and begged for you, so firmly and with all his heart, that I could not say him no in anything.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: non lo levanté, 'no lo inicié, no lo hice', 'I did not start it, I did not do it'. sabet, imperative, 'know' (the final -d spelt -t). pedidas vos ha e rogadas, 'he has you asked-for and begged-for': the participles agree with vos, the daughters, as in vos he casadas (v. 2189). Pidal's note: rogadas, remember that the king was the rogador of the marriage, the one who asked for it (v. 2080). atan = tan, 'so'; firme mientre, 'firmly', the adverb ending -mientre (= -mente) still written as a separate word. nulla cosa, 'nothing' (Latin nulla); nol = non le, 'not to him': with nulla, a double negative. sope = supe, 'I knew how to, could'. dezir de no, 'to say no'.

sentences.t:
Metivos en sus manos, fijas, amas ados;
bien me lo creades, que él vos casa, ca non yo.”
sentences.l:
I-put-you in his hands, daughters, both two;
well to-me it believe, that he you marries, and-not I.”
sentences.i: I have put you into his hands, my daughters, both of you; believe me well: it is he who gives you in marriage, not I.”
sentences.n: Metivos = metí + vos, 'I put you' (metí, preterite of meter). en sus manos: the Çid gave his daughters into the king's hands at the meeting (afellas en vuestra mano, v. 2088). amas ados = ambas a dos, 'both the two', as amas a dos at v. 1902. creades, present subjunctive as a polite command, 'may you believe'. él vos casa, ca non yo, 'it is he who marries you, and not I': ca non here is 'and not', setting the two against each other, as the glossary's ca non 'and not that' at v. 1839 (Pidal 'y no que'); not the usual causal ca 'for'. Tirada 110 ends here.

sentences.t:
Penssaron de adobar essora el palaçio,
por el suelo e suso tan bien encortinado,
tanta pórpola e tanto xámed e tanto paño preciado.
sentences.l:
They-thought to adorn then the palace,
through the floor and above so well tapestried,
so-much purple and so-much samite and so-much cloth precious.
sentences.i: Then they set about adorning the palace, hung so well with tapestries on the floor and above: so much purple, so much samite, so much costly cloth.
sentences.n: Tirada 111 (assonance á-o) — the weddings: preparations, the Infantes presented, Minaya gives the brides to the Infantes, blessings and mass, fifteen days of festivities, the weddings end with gifts to the guests, the juglar takes leave of his hearers (Pidal: Preparativos de las bodas.—Presentación de los infantes.—Minaya entrega las esposas a los infantes.—Bendiciones y misa.—Fiestas durante quince días.—Las bodas acaban; regalos a los convidados.—El juglar se despide de sus oyentes). The line-ends run palaçio, encortinado, preciado …: stressed á, then o. Penssaron de adobar, pensar de + infinitive, 'they set about adorning' (adobar, 'to fit out, array'). essora, 'then' (= entonces). Pidal's note: encortinado, 'covered with hangings on the floor and on the walls'; hangings on walls had been used from very early times, but on the floor they were rather a luxury of the peoples of the East, which spread to France only with the crusades. suso, 'above'. Pidal's note: pórpola, 'púrpura', 'purple', purple-dyed stuff; xámed, 'tela de seda', a silk cloth (samite). tanta … tanto with the singular, 'so much'. preciado, without the cedilla, as printed.

sentences.t:
Sabor abriedes de se[e]r e de comer en el palaçio.
Todos s[o]s cavalleros apriessa son juntados.
sentences.l:
Pleasure you-would-have of to-sit and of to-eat in the palace.
All h[i]s knights in-haste are gathered.
sentences.i: You would have taken pleasure in sitting and dining in that palace. All his knights are quickly gathered.
sentences.n: Sabor abriedes, 'you would have pleasure', conditional of aver: the singer turns to his hearers, as with veriedes 'you would see'. se[e]r here is 'to sit' (seer, from Latin sedere), not 'to be'; the second e is Pidal's. s[o]s = sus, 'his', the o Pidal's (so again at vv. 2214, 2243, 2265, 2273). apriessa, 'in haste'. son juntados, 'are gathered', ser with the participle.

sentences.t:
Por iffantes de Carrión essora enbiaron,
cavalgan los iffantes, adelant adeliñavan al palaçio,
con buenas vestiduras e fuertemientre adobados;
de pie e a sabor, Dios, qué quedos entraron!
sentences.l:
For infantes of Carrión then they-sent,
ride the infantes, forward they-made-straight to-the palace,
with good garments and mightily adorned;
of foot and at pleasure, God, how quiet they-entered!
sentences.i: Then they sent for the Infantes of Carrión. The Infantes mount and make their way straight on to the palace, in fine clothes and richly arrayed; they came in on foot and at their ease — God, how sedately they entered!
sentences.n: enbiar por, 'to send for'. iffantes, so spelt here with ff (ifantes elsewhere): the print's spellings kept. cavalgan … adeliñavan, present beside imperfect: the epic tense-mixing. adelant, 'forward'; adeliñar, 'to make straight for'. Pidal's note: fuertemientre adobados, 'muy bien ataviados', 'very well attired', that is, 'con lujo', 'in luxury'. de pie, 'on foot': they dismount and enter walking. a sabor, 'at (their) pleasure', at ease, unhurried. quedos, 'quiet, still', composed in bearing. Dios, qué …, the singer's exclamation, as at v. 2243.

sentences.i: My Çid received them with all his vassals; they bowed before him and before his wife, and went to sit on a costly bench.
sentences.n: Reçibiólos = reçibió + los, 'he received them'. el[l]e = él, with the old extra final -e; the second l is Pidal's. ssu = su, the s doubled after the vowel, as printed. se le omillaron, 'they bowed to him' (omillarse, 'to bow, greet', Pidal 'saludarle'; compare v. 2052, where the Infantes bowed to the Çid at the meeting). delant, 'before (them)'. ivan posar, ir + infinitive without a, 'they went to sit'. escaño, 'bench, settle', a seat of honour (as at v. 1762).

sentences.t:
Todos los de mio Çid tan bien son acordados,
están parando mientes al que en buen ora nasco.
El Campeador en pie es levantado:
sentences.l:
All those of my Çid so well are advised,
they-are setting minds on-him who in good hour was-born.
The Campeador on foot is risen:
sentences.i: All my Çid's men are so well schooled: they keep their eyes on him who was born in a good hour. The Campeador has risen to his feet:
sentences.n: Pidal's note: acordado, 'prudente', 'sensible, discreet' (compare v. 1290): his men know how to behave and wait on the Çid's word. están parando mientes, 'they are paying heed', parar mientes, 'to set the mind' (mientes, 'mind, attention'); estar + gerund for a continuing action. al que en buen ora nasco, the en buen ora formula, 'him who was born in a good hour'; nasco, the old strong preterite of naçer (= nació). en pie es levantado, 'is risen on his feet', ser with the participle.

sentences.i: “Since it is to be done, why do we keep delaying it? Come here, Álvar Fáñez, you whom I hold dear and love! Here are both my daughters; I place them in your hand;
sentences.n: a fazer lo avemos, 'we have it to do', aver a + infinitive, 'to have to'. Pidal's note: 'por qué lo vamos retardando?', 'why do we go on delaying it?'; imos = vamos, 'we go', ir + gerund for a continuing action. Venit, imperative, 'come' (final -d spelt -t). Álbar Fáñez is Minaya, named by the king to give the brides away in his stead (vv. 2131–2140). quiero e amo, 'I hold dear and love', a doubled phrase. Pidal's note: affé amas mis fijas, 'he aquí ambas mis hijas', 'here are both my daughters' (affé = afé, 'behold'). métolas = meto + las, 'I put them'.

sentences.t:
sabedes que al rey assí gelo he mandado,
no lo quiero fallir por nada de quanto ay parado:
a ifantes de Carrión dadlas con vuestra mano,
e prendan bendiçiones e vavamos recabdando.”
sentences.l:
you-know that to-the king thus to-him-it I-have granted,
not it I-want to-fail for nothing of all-that there-is settled:
to infantes of Carrión give-them with your hand,
and let-them-take blessings and let-us-go dispatching.”
sentences.i: you know that I have promised it so to the king, and I will not fall short in anything of all that has been agreed: give them with your hand to the Infantes of Carrión, and let them receive the blessings, and let us get this done.”
sentences.n: Pidal's note: 'así se lo he otorgado, o prometido', 'so I have granted, or promised, it to him': mandar, here 'to grant, promise' (as at v. 2148), not 'to command'. gelo = ge + lo, 'it to him' (modern se lo). Pidal's note: 'no quiero faltar en nada de cuanto se halla concertado con el rey', 'I will not fail in anything of all that is agreed with the king': fallir, 'to fail, fall short'; ay = hay, 'there is'; parado, 'settled, arranged'. a ifantes, without the article, as usual. dadlas = dad + las, 'give them' (here without the swap of daldas, v. 2136). Pidal's note: 'reciban la bendición y vayamos despachando esto', 'let them receive the blessing and let us get on with this': prendan, subjunctive of prender, 'take'; vavamos is so printed (Pidal's paraphrase has vayamos, 'let us go'); recabdar, 'to carry through, dispatch'.

sentences.t:
—Estoz dixo Minaya: “esto faré yo de grado.”
Levántanse derechas e metiógelas en mano.
A ifantes de Carrión Minaya va fablando:
sentences.l:
—Then said Minaya: “this will-do I with pleasure.”
They-rise-themselves upright and he-put-to-him-them in hand.
To infantes of Carrión Minaya goes speaking:
sentences.i: Then Minaya said: “This I will do gladly.” The ladies rise to their feet, and the Çid gave them into Minaya's hand. Minaya speaks to the Infantes of Carrión:
sentences.n: Estoz, 'then' (= entonces). de grado, 'gladly'. Pidal's note: the daughters stand up and the Çid gives them into Minaya's hands, who, holding them by the hand, speaks to the Infantes. Levántanse derechas, 'they rise upright', the daughters (derechas agrees with them). metiógelas = metió + ge + las, 'he (the Çid) put them to him (Minaya)', into his hand (ge singular here): the enclitic squeeze, ge as at v. 2223. va fablando, ir + gerund: 'speaks'. fablar = hablar, f- for h-.

sentences.t:
“Afevos delant Minaya, amos sodes hermanos.
Por mano del rey Alfons, que a mí lo ovo mandado,
dovos estas dueñas, —amas son fijas dalgo,—
que las tomassedes por mugieres a ondra e a recabdo.”
sentences.l:
“Behold-you before Minaya, both you-are brothers.
By hand of-the king Alfons, who to me it had commanded,
I-give-you these ladies, —both are daughters of-something,—
that them you-should-take as wives with honour and with care.”
sentences.i: “Here before you stands Minaya; you are brothers, the two of you. By the hand of King Alfonso, who gave me this charge, I give you these ladies — both are of noble birth — that you take them as your wives, with honour and in due form.”
sentences.n: Afevos = afé + vos, 'behold, here is', the presentative: Minaya points to himself, delant, 'before you'. amos sodes hermanos, 'you are both brothers': two brothers are given two sisters. sodes = sois. Por mano del rey, 'by the king's hand': Minaya acts as his proxy. mí, so accented as printed. ovo mandado, aver + participle, 'had commanded'. dovos = do + vos, 'I give you' (do = doy). fijas dalgo, 'daughters of something', of substance and lineage: noble ladies. tomassedes, imperfect subjunctive after the present: 'that you should take'. a ondra e a recabdo, 'with honour and with due care' (recabdo, 'good order', as at v. 2141). Pidal's note: Minaya hands over the brides as the king's representative (v. 2137), performing the civil ceremony of the marriage before the religious one; the Church sought to have the bride given over by the hand of the priest, who received her from the hand of her kin.

sentences.t:
Amos las reçiben d' amor e de grado,
a mio Çid e a su mugier van besar la mano.
sentences.l:
Both them receive with love and with pleasure,
to my Çid and to his wife they-go to-kiss the hand.
sentences.i: The two receive them lovingly and gladly, and go to kiss the hands of my Çid and his wife.
sentences.n: Amos = ambos, 'both', the Infantes. d' amor = de amor, the vowel elided, printed with a space. van besar, ir + infinitive without a. la mano, singular, for each of the two.

sentences.t:
Quando ovieron aquesto fecho, salieron del palacio,
pora Santa María a priessa adelinnando;
sentences.l:
When they-had this done, they-went-out from-the palace,
for Santa María in haste making-straight;
sentences.i: When they had done this, they left the palace and made in haste for Santa María;
sentences.n: ovieron … fecho, aver + participle, 'had done' (fecho = hecho, f- for h-). aquesto = esto. palacio, without the cedilla here, as printed (palaçio at v. 2205). Santa María is here the church of Valencia, Don Jerome's see, not the cathedral of Burgos of v. 52. a priessa, 'in haste'. adelinnando = adeliñando, 'making straight for', nn written for ñ.

sentences.i: the bishop, Don Jerome, vested himself in all haste and was waiting for them at the church door; he gave them the blessings and sang the mass.
sentences.n: Jero[me], the me Pidal's (in italics), as before. vistiós = vistió + se, 'vested himself', the -se worn to -s. Pidal's note: tan privado, 'tan de prisa', 'in such haste'. sediellos sperando = sedié + los + esperando, 'he was waiting for them' (seer + gerund, a continuing action); sperando = esperando. eclegia, here with one c, ecclegia at v. 2241: both as printed. The blessing is given at the church door, then the mass within. bendictiones, a Latin spelling. dióles, preterite, then a cantado = ha cantado, a perfect: tense-mixing.

sentences.t:
Al salir de la ecclegia cavalgaron tan privado,
a la glera de Valençia fuera dieron salto;
Dios, qué bien tovieron armas el Çid e s[o]s vassallos!
Tres cavallos cameó el que en buen ora nasco.
sentences.l:
At-the going-out from the church they-rode so quickly,
to the gravel-bank of Valençia outside they-gave leap;
God, how well they-held arms the Çid and h[i]s vassals!
Three horses changed he who in good hour was-born.
sentences.i: As they came out of the church they mounted in all haste and sallied out to the river-flats of Valencia; God, how well the Çid and his vassals played at arms! He who was born in a good hour changed horses three times.
sentences.n: tan privado again, 'in all haste'. glera, 'gravel-bank, river shingle', the open flats beside the river outside the walls, the ground for the games. fuera dieron salto, 'they leapt out', sallied forth (compare de Valençia dieron salto, v. 1716). Pidal's note: tovieron armas, 'jugaron las armas', 'they played at arms', mock combat on horseback (compare v. 1577). tovieron = tuvieron. cameó, 'changed' (camear = cambiar, compare camearon at v. 2093), so printed; he rode three horses hard in the games. el que en buen ora nasco, the formula again.

sentences.t:
Mio Çid de lo que vi[d]ie mucho era pagado:
ifantes de Carrión bien an cavalgado.
sentences.l:
My Çid of that which he-saw much was pleased:
infantes of Carrión well have ridden.
sentences.i: My Çid was much pleased with what he saw: the Infantes of Carrión have ridden well.
sentences.n: vi[d]ie = veía, 'saw, was seeing', the old imperfect of ver (Latin videbat); the d Pidal's. pagado, 'pleased, satisfied' (pagar, 'to please'). an cavalgado, 'have ridden': the Infantes acquit themselves well in the games, and the Çid sees it.

sentences.t:
Tórnanse con las dueñas, a Valençia an entrado;
ricas fueron las bodas en el alcaç[er] ondrado,
sentences.l:
They-turn-themselves with the ladies, into Valençia they-have entered;
rich were the weddings in the citadel honoured,
sentences.i: They come back with the ladies; they have entered Valencia. Rich were the weddings in the honoured citadel,
sentences.n: Tórnanse, 'they return' (tornarse), present, then an entrado, perfect, then fueron, preterite: tense-mixing. alcaç[er], 'citadel, fortress', the er Pidal's (unaccented here, alcáç[er] at v. 2183). ondrado, 'honoured'.

sentences.t:
e al otro día fizo mio Çid fincar siete tablados:
antes que entrassen a yantar todos los [cr]ebantaron.
sentences.l:
and at-the other day made my Çid plant seven board-castles:
before that they-should-enter to dine all them they-broke.
sentences.i: and the next day my Çid had seven board castles set up; before they went in to dine they had broken down every one.
sentences.n: al otro día, 'on the next day'. fizo … fincar, 'had (them) set up', fazer + infinitive as a causative; fincar, 'to plant, set firm'. Pidal's note here is only 'tablados, v. 1602', where the knights at play broke tablados: a tablado was a little castle of boards which the knights struck with their lances to bring it down. [cr]ebantaron = quebrantaron, 'broke', the cr Pidal's. yantar, 'to dine' (the midday meal).

sentences.t:
Quinze días conplidos en las bodas duraron,
çerca de los quinze días yas van los fijos dalgo.
sentences.l:
Fifteen days full in the weddings they-spent,
near of the fifteen days now-themselves go the sons of-something.
sentences.i: Fifteen full days they spent on the weddings; toward the end of the fifteen days the nobles take their leave.
sentences.n: Pidal's note: duraron, 'emplearon, gastaron', 'they spent' (compare v. 1169); weddings commonly lasted one or two weeks, and up to five and seven, so much so that in the thirteenth century the laws had to put limits on such costly festivities. conplidos, 'complete, full'. yas van = ya se van, 'now they go away'. fijos dalgo, 'noblemen', the guests.

sentences.i: My Çid Don Rodrigo, he who was born in a good hour, in palfreys and mules and swift horses — in beasts alone — has given away a hundred;
sentences.n: don Rodrigo, the Çid's own name. entre … e …, 'between … and …', counting the kinds together. palafrés, 'palfreys', easy-paced riding horses; mulas, for the road or for burden; cavallos corredores, 'running horses', swift war-horses. en bestias sines al, 'in beasts, without anything else': sines = sin, al, 'other thing' (lo al, v. 2173): in mounts alone, before the clothes and the coin of the next lines. çiento, 'a hundred', without article. The line is terse and Pidal has no note on it. [ha], the word Pidal's (in italics). mandados, 'given, bestowed' (mandar, 'to grant', as at vv. 2148, 2223), agreeing with the hundred beasts.

sentences.t:
mantos e pelliçones e otros vestidos largos;
non f[o]ron en cuenta los ave[r]es monedados.
sentences.l:
mantles and fur-tunics and other garments long;
not w[e]re in count the goods coined.
sentences.i: mantles and fur-lined tunics and other garments in plenty; the wealth in coin was past counting.
sentences.n: pelliçones, 'fur-lined tunics' (compare pelliza). Pidal's note: vestidos largos, 'vestidos en abundancia', 'garments in abundance' (compare v. 804), not 'long garments'. non f[o]ron en cuenta, 'were not in the count', past counting (non son en cuenta, vv. 918, 1983); f[o]ron = fueron, the o Pidal's. ave[r]es monedados, 'coined wealth', money in struck coin; the r Pidal's.

sentences.t:
Los vassallos de mio Çid assí son acordados,
cada uno por sí sos dones avien dados.
sentences.l:
The vassals of my Çid thus are agreed,
each one for himself his gifts had given.
sentences.i: My Çid's vassals were of one mind in this: each of them, on his own account, had given gifts of his own.
sentences.n: son acordados: here most likely 'are agreed, of one mind' (acordar, 'to agree'), though the 'well-advised' of v. 2217 is possible too. por sí, 'for his own part'. sos dones, 'his gifts' (sos = sus). avien dados, 'had given', the participle agreeing with dones. Pidal's note: not only the father but the kinsmen and friends of the bride gave lavishly to all who were bidden to the wedding.

sentences.t:
Qui aver quiere prender bien era abastado;
ricos tornan a Castiella los que a las bodas llegaron.
sentences.l:
Who wealth wishes to-take well was supplied;
rich they-return to Castiella those who to the weddings came.
sentences.i: Whoever wished to take wealth was well supplied; rich they go home to Castile, those who came to the weddings.
sentences.n: Qui, 'whoever'. aver, the noun, 'wealth'. prender = tomar, 'to take'. abastado, 'supplied, provided' (abastar). quiere … era, tornan … llegaron: present and past side by side, tense-mixing. Castiella = Castilla.

sentences.t:
Yas ivan partiendo aquestos ospedados,
espidiéndos de R[o]y Díaz, el que en buen ora nasco,
e a todas las dueñas e a los fijos dalgo;
por pagados se parten de mio Çid e de s[o]s vassallos.
sentences.l:
Now-themselves were departing these guests,
taking-leave-themselves of R[o]y Díaz, he who in good hour was-born,
and to all the ladies and to the sons of-something;
for satisfied themselves they-part from my Çid and from h[i]s vassals.
sentences.i: Now these guests were departing, taking their leave of Ruy Díaz, he who was born in a good hour, and of all the ladies and the noblemen; they part from my Çid and his vassals well content.
sentences.n: Yas = ya + se. ivan partiendo, ir + gerund, 'were departing'. ospedados, 'the lodged ones', the guests (at v. 247 ospedado was 'lodging'). espidiéndos = espidiéndose, 'taking leave' (espedirse = despedirse), the -se worn to -s. R[o]y Díaz = Ruy Díaz, only the o Pidal's. Pidal's note: note the mixed construction, espedirse de (de Roy Díaz) and espedirse a (a todas las dueñas). por pagados se parten, 'they part as satisfied', content with their welcome and their gifts.

sentences.t: Grant bien dizen dellos ca será aguisado.
sentences.l: Great good they-say of-them for it-will-be fitting.
sentences.i: They speak great good of them, as is only right.
sentences.n: dellos = de ellos, 'of them', the Çid and his vassals. ca será aguisado, 'for it will be fitting': the future of what must be so, 'as well it may be'; aguisado, 'fitting, right'.

sentences.t:
Mucho eran alegres Di[da]go e Ferrando;
estos f[o]ron fijos del co[m]de don Gonçal[v]o.
sentences.l:
Much were glad Di[da]go and Ferrando;
these w[e]re sons of-the co[u]nt don Gonçal[v]o.
sentences.i: Diego and Fernando were full of joy; these were the sons of Count Don Gonzalo.
sentences.n: Di[da]go, the da Pidal's (in italics): Didago, the older form of Diego; Ferrando = Fernando. They are the Infantes of Carrión. f[o]ron = fueron. co[m]de = conde, the m Pidal's; Gonçal[v]o, the v Pidal's: their father, Count Gonzalo, whose name the patronymic of their brother Asur González carries (v. 2172).

sentences.t:
Venidos son a Castiella aquestos ospedados,
el Çid e sos hyernos en Valençia son rastados.
sentences.l:
Come are to Castiella these guests,
the Çid and his sons-in-law in Valençia are remained.
sentences.i: These guests have come home to Castile; the Çid and his sons-in-law have stayed on in Valencia.
sentences.n: Venidos son, 'have come', ser as the auxiliary of a verb of motion. aquestos = estos. Pidal's note: son rastados, 'han quedado', 'have remained' (rastar, 'to stay behind'; compare a rastado at v. 1733). hyernos = yernos, 'sons-in-law', the h only a spelling. sos = sus.

sentences.t:
Y moran los ifantes bien cerca de dos años,
los amores que les fazen mucho eran sobejanos.
Alegre era el Çid e todos s[o]s vassallos.
sentences.l:
There dwell the infantes well near of two years,
the loves that to-them they-do much were excessive.
Glad was the Çid and all h[i]s vassals.
sentences.i: There the Infantes dwell for close on two years, and the kindnesses shown them were beyond all measure. Glad was the Çid, and all his vassals.
sentences.n: Y, 'there' (= allí). moran, 'they dwell', present, then eran, past: tense-mixing. bien cerca de, 'well nigh'; cerca without the cedilla here, as printed (çerca at v. 2252). Pidal's note: 'los agasajos que les hacen', 'the attentions paid them': amores, 'kindnesses, warm attentions', not love in the modern sense. sobejanos, 'excessive, beyond measure'.

sentences.t:
¡Plega a Santa María e al Padre santo
ques pague des casamiento mio Çid o el que lo ovo âlgo.
sentences.l:
May-it-please to Saint Mary and to-the Father holy
that-himself be-pleased of-that marriage my Çid or he who it held at-something.
sentences.i: May it please Holy Mary and the Holy Father that my Çid, or he who prized this match, have joy of that marriage.
sentences.n: The singer's prayer: Pidal opens it with ¡ and closes it with a full stop, as printed. Plega, present subjunctive of plazer, 'may it please'. ques = que + se. pague … de, 'be pleased with' (pagarse de). des = de + es, 'of that', es the shortened ese (as en es día, v. 1678). Pidal's note: o el que lo ovo âlgo, 'o el que lo estimó en algo', 'or he who held it in some esteem', a phrase that no doubt alludes to the king, the one who asked for the marriage; but the reading is very doubtful, the manuscript being damaged at this point. âlgo carries Pidal's circumflex for two words run together, a + algo (aver a algo, 'to hold in esteem'), as with ên, lâ. Pidal adds that the juglar makes as if he did not know the fate that awaits the Çid's daughters, to keep his hearers' interest awake.

sentences.t:
Las coplas deste cantar aquis van acabando.
El Criador vos vala con todos los sos santos.
sentences.l:
The verses of-this song here-themselves go ending.
The Creator you may-aid with all the his saints.
sentences.i: The verses of this song are here coming to an end. May the Creator keep you, with all his saints.
sentences.n: Here the second cantar, the Cantar de las bodas ('the Song of the Weddings'), ends with the juglar's leave-taking (Pidal's rubric: El juglar se despide de sus oyentes); the third, the Cantar de la afrenta de Corpes, begins with the next tirada. coplas, 'verses, stanzas'. aquis = aquí + se. van acabando, ir + gerund, 'are coming to an end'. vala, present subjunctive of valer, 'may (he) protect', the blessing the girl of Burgos gave the Çid at v. 48; los sos santos, article + possessive (sos = sus), as at v. 2149. Tirada 111 ends here, and with it the second cantar.
